big: Meena has ₹6 lakh to lend. Instead of putting it all in one five-year deposit, she splits it into three parts maturing in one, three and five years. Every year or two, some money comes back, ready to be used or reinvested.

lines: Why split it? One deposit is simpler.
A ladder gives you money back at regular intervals, and spreads the risk of reinvesting at the wrong time. It is a way of not betting everything on one date or one rate.

small: at each rung of the ladder
alt: Three equal bars showing money returning in years one, three and five
caps: Meena splits ₹6 lakh into three equal parts.
One part matures in the first year.
The last matures in year five. Money returns at regular intervals.

rows: Fixed interest for a set time, insured up to a limit per bank
A company bond that cannot be converted into shares
Interest resets with a benchmark rate
Bonds of different maturities, so money returns in steps
note: Deposit insurance covers up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank, including interest. NCDs and company deposits are not covered the same way.

q: Rohan splits money into bonds maturing in 1, 3 and 5 years. What is this called?
why: Bonds of different maturities form a ladder.
A split is a share action, not a way of holding bonds.
A bonus issue gives extra shares, not maturities.
A sum insured is an insurance term, not a bond.

q: A bank holds a depositor's ₹8 lakh in one account. If the bank fails, how much is insured, as a rule?
why: The cover has a limit, so not all ₹8 lakh is insured.
Bank deposits are insured up to a limit, so not nothing.
Deposit insurance covers up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank.
₹50 lakh is far above the insured limit.

opts: A bank savings account that earns interest
A government treasury bill for a year
A share that pays no dividend at all
why: A savings account is held with a bank and is not a bond.
A treasury bill is issued by the government.
An NCD is a bond, so it is not a share.
A non-convertible debenture is a company bond that stays debt.

q: Meena's floating rate bond pays interest linked to a benchmark. Rates rise. What happens to her coupon?
opts: It stays fixed for ever and ever
why: A rise in the benchmark does not lower a floating rate.
A floating rate resets with the benchmark, so it rises.
A fixed rate bond stays fixed, but a floating one does not.
A rate change does not cancel the coupon.

pts: A ladder returns money in steps, and spreads the reinvestment risk.
Deposit insurance is up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank.
An NCD is a company bond, and carries credit risk.
